blocks.text: …died during that evacuation. And their families were never told the truth about how."
The investigator's name was Dr. Linda Marsh. She'd been looking for proof for three years.

When the hurricane hit, a private nursing home on the coast was ordered to evacuate. Its owner contracted a cheap transport company to move forty-two residents inland. The company didn't have enough ambulances, so it sent this vehicle: an old ambulance it had converted years earlier to carry bodies for funeral homes. No oxygen equipment. No working air conditioning. No medical staff, just a driver.

Six of the most fragile patients, including two children from the facility's pediatric wing who depended on ventilators, were loaded into it. The drive took nine hours in traffic and heat. All six died before they reached the receiving facility.
The nursing home's owner and the transport company falsified the records.

The paperwork showed all forty-two residents "successfully transferred." The six deaths were listed as having occurred days later, of natural causes, at the new facility. A doctor who worked for the owner signed the death certificates.
The driver couldn't live with it. Before he quit, he hid the six wristbands under the floor panel, hoping someone would find them. Three years later, someone did.

Dr. Marsh's investigation took eleven months. The driver came forward once he learned the wristbands had been found. The nursing home's owner, the transport company's owner, and the doctor who signed the certificates were charged with manslaughter and fraud. The nursing home lost its license.
The families learned what really happened. One of them, the mother of a nine-year-old boy named Daniel, asked to meet me. She told me she'd always felt something was wrong.
Her son had been stable when they told her he was being moved. Three days later, she was told he'd "passed peacefully" in a new facility she'd never been allowed to visit.
"I needed to know he wasn't alone with strangers lying about him," she said. "You gave me the truth."
The state passed a new law the following year requiring licensed medical transport for every nursing home evacuation. Families call it Daniel's Law.
I still restore emergency vehicles. I check under every floor panel.
